The President’s Budget Request is just that, a request. To compensate for years of underfunding, the Administration proposes to increase defense funding significantly and recognizes the annual appropriations process as the best way to provide additional funds. The request for just one DDG-51, the workhorse of the U.S. Navy, is insufficient to counter the ever-growing Chinese fleet, which now exceeds the size of the American Navy, as well as other global threats.  
 
While there are some improvements over last year’s domestic discretionary budget request, including full support for the Pell Grant program, the request has several shortcomings. For example, the proposal includes unwarranted funding cuts in biomedical research.  It would also terminate worthwhile programs like LIHEAP, which helps low-income families and seniors to pay their energy bills during the cold winter and hot summer months, and TRIO, which assists low-income, first-generation students in pursuing higher education.  Job Corps, which helps students from troubled backgrounds gain the skills and education they need to enter the workforce, join the military, or pursue higher education, would also be phased out.  These are proven programs that I strongly support.
 
Another program that is important to rural America’s economy is the Essential Air Service program.  The Administration is proposing deep cuts in the EAS program.    
 
After careful review, Congress decisively rejected these particular cuts last year.
 
While the Administration proposes a budget, Congress holds the power of the purse. The Senate Appropriations Committee will now hold hearings with cabinet members and agency heads to review these recommendations and to explore other fiscally responsible proposals.  I hope my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, who too often worked over the last year to impede the appropriations process and shut down federal agencies, will abandon their harmful tactics and work with us to govern responsibly.

During Women's History Month, I would like to recognize a leader and humanitarian from Southwest Georgia, Lillian Gordy Carter.

Born in Richland, Georgia, in 1898, she quickly gained recognition in her community for her diligent work as a nurse.

"Miss Lillian", as she was known, served in her local hospital, challenged the bigoted color barriers of the time, and raised four children with her husband James Earl Carter.

She played an active role in her son Jimmy's senate, governor, and presidential campaigns, where she gained nationwide recognition for her earnestness and Southern charm. Much like her son, Lillian continued to serve the public long after her retirement. After completing her career as a nurse at age 68, Lillian joined the Peace Corps, where she worked in a clinic in India.

As a powerful figure for progress, Lillian inspired a president and continues to be an inspiration to generations that have followed. From Plains, Georgia, to Godrej, India, her compassion touched the lives of many.

G000546.text:
When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

.@GlyphosateGirl says it best: Giving corporate interests a liability shield, especially when their products make people sick, is completely un-American.

RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

As part of our weekly series, my office is highlighting how our constituent services team works diligently to create a positive impact on the people of the Eighth District. 
James Colangelo is a Navy veteran. In 1985, Mr. Colangelo served on the USS Dale when a compartment on board flooded. He went to the flooded area to survey the damage. Mr. Colangelo became trapped in the tight space as it filled with seawater and fuel, leaving him completely submerged. He nearly drowned but survived. The incident left him with lifelong post-traumatic stress disorder as he continues to relive the terrifying day more than 40 years later.
Because of the incident, Mr. Colangelo filed a claim for disability benefits with the Department of Veterans Affairs but faced challenges. My staff contacted the VA and through my team’s hard work, the VA moved his disability rating to 100% giving him full coverage for his medical costs. The agency also granted him more than $4,000 a month in disability benefits and later agreed to give him an additional $20,000 in backpay.
“The help I received from this office was instrumental in receiving my VA benefits. [The caseworker] opened doors for me, allowing me to advocate for myself. I will always be grateful for all the help after three and half years of trying to get my benefits. Thank you!”
If you need help with a federal agency, you can contact my office at 847-413-1959 or at IL08.HelpLine@mail.house.gov.

Roger Sherman was a signer from Connecticut who not only signed the Declaration of Independence, but he also worked closely with Jefferson to draft the document. Roger was born into a poor family, but he worked his way out of debt and became a successful attorney. In addition to helping draft the Declaration of Independence, Roger Sherman also helped write the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution. He was one of six individuals to sign both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
